3.text: From a Greek harbour town, Rome ruled for nearly a thousand more years.

4.text: This is the Byzantine Empire: riots, plague, secret fire and betrayal by friends.

5.text: So why was a Roman emperor still fighting in 1453?

6.text: Our story starts in 330, when Constantine rebuilt Byzantion, on the Bosphorus, as "New Rome."

7.text: In 395, the empire split between two brothers, East and West.

8.text: Around 413, giant walls went up: 5.7 kilometres long, with 96 towers.

9.text: In 476, a warlord kicked out the last western emperor

10.text: and posted his crown and robes to Constantinople.

13.text: The walls could stop any army.

14.text: But the danger was inside, at the racetrack.

15.text: Under Justinian, chariot-racing fans belonged to rival gangs: the Blues and the Greens.

16.text: In 532, both gangs rioted, chanting "Nika!", and burned the city centre.

19.text: Empress Theodora said she'd rather die in imperial purple than run.

20.text: So General Belisarius sealed the Hippodrome gates.

21.text: Procopius claims about 30,000 people died inside.

22.text: Weeks later, work began on a new Hagia Sophia.

23.text: It opened in 537, with a dome 31 metres wide.

24.text: For nearly a thousand years, no cathedral on Earth was bigger.

25.text: Justinian also squeezed Roman law into one code.

26.text: Then his generals retook North Africa and Italy.

27.text: But in 541, plague struck, probably carried by rats on grain ships.

28.text: The wars and plague drained Rome,

29.text: just as a new power rose from the desert.

30.text: Arab armies took Syria in 636, then Egypt, the empire's breadbasket.

31.text: Twice, in 674 and 717, Arab forces besieged Constantinople.

32.text: The Romans answered with Greek fire: liquid flame that burned on water.

33.text: By 718, fire, frost and Bulgar raiders had shattered the attackers.

34.text: Later, Basil II, the Bulgar-Slayer, conquered Bulgaria.

35.text: A later chronicler claims he blinded 15,000 Bulgarian prisoners.

36.text: The empire's gold coin, the solidus, was the dollar of the Middle Ages.

37.text: But after Basil, the gold got watered down.

38.text: In 1071, at Manzikert, the Turks captured an emperor.

39.text: In 1204, a crusade steered by Venice's blind old leader

41.text: The Romans won it back 57 years later,

42.text: but a new enemy was waiting.

43.text: Then the final boss arrived: Sultan Mehmed II, aged 21.

44.text: He brought giant cannons built by a gunsmith named Orban.

45.text: He'd reportedly offered them to the Romans first, who couldn't pay.

46.text: Stone balls smashed walls that had held for a thousand years.

47.text: Mehmed dragged about 70 ships overland on greased logs, past the harbour chain.

48.text: About 7,000 defenders faced up to 80,000 attackers.

49.text: But here's the twist most people forget.

50.text: The last emperor was Constantine, son of Helena.

51.text: So was the city's first emperor, 1,123 years earlier.

53.text: Constantine XI died fighting, and his body was never identified.

56.text: Even Mehmed called himself "Caesar of Rome."

57.text: But in 1557, a German scholar popularised a new label: Byzantine.

58.text: So why does this matter today?

59.text: Fleeing Greek scholars carried ancient books to Italy, fuelling the Renaissance.

60.text: Orthodox Christianity and the Cyrillic alphabet spread north from Byzantium.

61.text: Russia adopted the double-headed eagle and called Moscow the "Third Rome."

62.text: Justinian's code still shapes civil law across Europe and Latin America.

63.text: Nobody who lived there ever called themselves Byzantine.

64.text: To the last man on the walls, they were Romans.

65.text: For more empires that refused to die, subscribe.
